caveats: We give educational estimates, not financial, tax or legal advice or a benefits decision.
We cover one person living alone, and leave out couples, additional amounts for severe disability or caring, and Savings Credit.

We leave out Housing Benefit and Council Tax Reduction. People on Guarantee Credit pass the income and capital tests for both automatically (SI 2006/214 reg 26; SI 2012/2885 Sch 1 para 13), so losing Guarantee Credit can cost more than this result shows.
We don’t cover Scottish taxpayers, who pay the income tax rates the Scottish Parliament sets.

We count Pension Credit in 52 weeks from Monday 6 April 2026, starting with the first week that begins on or after the day you reach Pension Credit age. DWP pays from your first full benefit week, which turns on your payday, unless you move straight from Universal Credit, Income Support, income-based Jobseeker’s Allowance or income-related Employment and Support Allowance (SI 1987/1968 reg 16A). If your State Pension age falls on or after 6 April 2010, DWP pays in arrears, weekly, fortnightly or every four weeks, on a day your National Insurance number sets unless it arranges another (reg 26BA). The tax year also has 52 weeks and a day, so the credit you get for 2026/27 can be about a week’s worth more or less than we show, some of it can arrive after 5 April 2027, and a claim that starts later pays less.

We assume you spend the money you draw evenly through the year. DWP can treat someone as still holding money they spent or gave away to get or increase Pension Credit (SI 2002/1792 regs 18(6) and 21).

We value an undrawn pot from the Government Actuary’s table, and DWP decision makers also weigh evidence from the pension provider (DMG 85470-85471). DWP decides whether withdrawals count as regular or one-off (DMG 85456-85457).

We count all of a regular withdrawal as income, its tax-free part included, reading DMG 85456 and 85476 that way. DMG 85472 treats a lump sum of up to 25% taken when income starts as capital; if DWP treats your tax-free part that way, Pension Credit here may be too low.
We take the tax payable on counted income off that income (SI 2002/1792 reg 17(10)) and take no tax off income DWP only assumes a pot produces.

If your State Pension age falls on or after 6 April 2010, DWP pays in arrears, weekly, fortnightly or every four weeks, on a day your National Insurance number sets unless it arranges another (reg 26BA). The tax year also has 52 weeks and a day, so the credit you get for 2026/27 can be about a week’s worth more or less than we show, some of it can arrive after 5 April 2027, and a claim that starts later pays less.

We assume you spend the money you draw evenly through the year. DWP can treat someone as still holding money they spent or gave away to get or increase Pension Credit (SI 2002/1792 regs 18(6) and 21).

We value an undrawn pot from the Government Actuary’s table, and DWP decision makers also weigh evidence from the pension provider (DMG 85470-85471). DWP decides whether withdrawals count as regular or one-off (DMG 85456-85457).

We count all of a regular withdrawal as income, its tax-free part included, reading DMG 85456 and 85476 that way. DMG 85472 treats a lump sum of up to 25% taken when income starts as capital; if DWP treats your tax-free part that way, Pension Credit here may be too low.
We take the tax payable on counted income off that income (SI 2002/1792 reg 17(10)) and take no tax off income DWP only assumes a pot produces.
